deep.reconstruction:
OVERALL SUBJECT. The page tabulates the classes of binary quadratic forms of determinant -p (in Gauss's notation: forms (a,b,c) = ax^2+2bxy+cy^2 with b^2-ac=-p; modern discriminant D=-4p). It covers primes p ≡ 5 (mod 8) and records how they decompose into sums of three squares. This is the computational side of Disquisitiones Arithmeticae arts. 288-292, where ternary forms x^2+y^2+z^2 are tied to binary forms of determinant -p.

THE ENTRY FORMAT 'p  o.h'. Example: 997 o.14.
- h is the number of (properly primitive) classes, h(-4p). The class group is cyclic in every case here.
- The classes are labelled by indices k = 0..h-1 with respect to a generating class.
- 'C.k.(h-k)' groups a class with its inverse, giving h/2+1 'Classes' in Gauss's sense.
- The last such class, C.h/2, is the ambiguous class (2,2,(p+1)/2). This is why every list ends 'C.h/2 c:2'.
- After 'c' Gauss writes a small number (usually a prime) represented by that class. These are his 'multiplicatores'.
- Next to the even indices (the principal genus) he writes a decomposition of p into three squares.

BLOCK 1 (top left). This is the tail of an entry begun on a lost or earlier sheet; it is not the 373 of the previous page. The decomposition 576+196+81 = 24^2+14^2+9^2 = 853 identifies it as p = 853, h = 10. The lines read:
- C.1.9 c:7
- C.2.8 (blotted; almost certainly 484+225+144 = 22^2+15^2+12^2)
- C.3.7 c:
- C.4.6 576+196+81
- C.5 c:2
C.0 (hidden by the blot) must be 529+324 = 23^2+18^2.
Check (mine): 853 has exactly 3 decompositions, (0,18,23), (12,15,22), (9,14,24), so n = 3 and h = 4n-2 = 10. Also 7 is represented, since -853 ≡ 1 (mod 7).

BLOCK 2: 877 o.10. Only the skeleton C.0, C.1.9, C.2.8, C.3.7, C.4.6, C.5 is written. The decompositions (mine) are 841+36, 729+144+4 and 441+400+36, so n = 3 and h = 10.

BLOCK 3: 941 o.38. Skeleton C.0 ... C.19, i.e. 20 = h/2+1 classes. One multiplier is given: C.1.37 c:3, and -941 ≡ 1 (mod 3) is a square. h = 38 implies n = 10 decompositions; equivalently r3(941) = 456.

BLOCK 4: 997 o.14. Fully worked:
- C.0: 36+961 = 6^2+31^2 (+0^2), c:1
- C.1.13: c.43
- C.2.12: 16+81+900 = 4^2+9^2+30^2, c.73
- C.3.11: c.11
- C.4.10: 196+225+576 = 14^2+15^2+24^2, c.53
- C.5.9: c.7
- C.6.8: 144+324+529 = 12^2+18^2+23^2, c.13
- C.7: c:2
The 4 decompositions sit at the 4 principal-genus pairs {0}, {2,12}, {4,10}, {6,8}.

Checks on block 4 (mine):
- The 48+48+48+24 signed/ordered representations give r3(997) = 168 = 12·14.
- The genus character (·/997) is +1 on 13, 53, 73 (even indices) and -1 on 7, 11, 43 (odd indices).
- Composition test: the class of 43 is (43,11,26) ~ (26,-11,43). Its duplicate reduces as (1849,-376,77) -> (77,-9,14) -> (14,-5,73), a form representing 73. So class(43)^2 = class(73), confirming the indices 1 and 2.

BOTTOM TABLE. All primes p ≡ 5 (mod 8) up to 1013 are sorted by h(-4p): 2, 6, 10, 14, 18, 22, 26, 30, 34, 38. Spot checks (mine) via h = 4n-2 confirm, for example:
- 5, 13, 37: n = 1
- 29, 53, 61: n = 2
- 101: n = 4, h = 14
- 613: n = 3, h = 10
The marginal '46' is unexplained. It is not the table count, which is 44 entries.

ANNOTATION (Ann.), modern paraphrase. Let n be the number of essentially different decompositions of p into three squares.
- p ≡ 5 (mod 8): exactly one decomposition has a zero (p = a^2+b^2) and none has two equal terms. So r3(p) = 24+48(n-1) = 12(4n-2). With Gauss's r3(p) = 12h(-4p) this gives h = 4n-2 indices and (h/2)+1 = 2n classes. This is exactly what the page shows.
- p ≡ 1 (mod 8): Gauss writes 2n classes and 4n indices; the '2n-1' was corrected. This matches the data only if n excludes the decomposition containing a zero. Examples: 17 -> {9+4+4}, h = 4; 41 -> {36+4+1, 16+16+9}, h = 8.
- p ≡ 3 (mod 8): there is one decomposition a^2+2b^2 and no zero. So r3 = 48n-24 = 24h(-p), giving h(-p) = 2n-1 and h(-4p) = 3h(-p) = 6n-3 indices and 3n-1 classes.
- The number 4 (i.e. the form (4,±1 or 2,·)) always falls in the classes with indices 2n-1 and 4n-2, the subgroup of order 3 (kernel of the map from det -p forms to the maximal order).
- If squares of fractions with denominator 4 are admitted (passing to discriminant -p), indices merge in triples. Their number becomes 2n-1 and the classes become n.

The next page begins precisely this 8n+3 part ('Pars 3').
errors: Bottom table: 613 appears twice, under h=10 and under h=30. The h=10 entry is correct (613 has exactly 3 decompositions: (0,17,18), (1,6,24), (8,15,18)). The entry under 30 is wrong. The prime 821 ≡ 5 (mod 8) is missing from the table, so the h=30 entry was presumably meant to be 821 (to verify: h(-3284)=30), unless the image actually reads 821.

Annotation: n is not defined uniformly. For 8k+5, h = 4n-2 requires n to include the decomposition with a zero term (997: n=4). For 8k+1, the stated '4n indices' requires n to exclude it (17: h=4; 41: h=8). Under the single stated definition 'n = number of distinct decompositions into 3 squares', the 8k+1 case should read 4n-4 indices and 2n-1 classes, which is the struck-out '2n-1'.
Marginal '46' does not match the number of table entries (44) or any visible quantity; meaning unclear.
No arithmetic errors found in the 997 or 853 entries: all decompositions sum correctly, and all multipliers satisfy -p ≡ square (mod q) with the genus parity matching the index parity.

results.what: For prime p≡5 (mod 8): h(-4p) = 4n-2, where n is the number of decompositions of p into three squares; the decompositions correspond to pairs of inverse classes in the principal genus
results.modern_name: Gauss's three-square theorem r3(p)=12h(-4p) (special case), with the correspondence between representations by x^2+y^2+z^2 and classes of the principal genus

results.what: For p≡3 (mod 8): h(-4p)=6n-3=3h(-p); the form 4 lies in the order-3 subgroup (indices 2n-1, 4n-2); denominators 4 give h(-p)=2n-1
results.modern_name: Relation h(-4p)=3h(-p) for p≡3 mod 8 (order index formula), r3(p)=24h(-p)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (DA arts. 253-256, 291-292); later Dirichlet's class number formula

results.what: Table of class numbers h(-4p) for all primes p≡5 mod 8 up to 1013, with explicit cyclic indexing of classes by a generator and representative primes
results.modern_name: Class number tables / index (discrete logarithm) tables in cyclic class groups
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (class number tables published posthumously in Werke II)

deep.surprise_reason: This is Gauss's own published theory (DA arts. 291-292) applied computationally, in the style of his known class-number tables in Werke II. The only non-routine features are the cyclic index labelling and the explicit uniform counting rules for the three residue classes mod 8, both consistent with his known work.
